nh_airation_buttress.blurb: A pale granite buttress perched at the very top of Cathedral Ledge, above the Thin Air face. Climbers start from a broad, tree-covered ledge roughly 400 feet off the ground, so even the first moves feel airy. The routes are mostly trad with a couple of sport lines, and the bulk of them fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with a few easier lines mixed in. Several routes can be reached from the ledge without roping up, while the far left side calls for a roped traverse. Some lines on the wall dry quickly after rain, which helps on unsettled days.
nh_airation_buttress.parking_note: Drive the summit road and leave the car on the shoulder near the top; a trail leads from there around to the ledge above the cliff.

nh_wiswall_boulders_aka_thompson_farm.blurb: A small cluster of boulders in the woods near Durham, tucked on university-owned land beside a network of trails. The problems run from V0 into the V5 and V6 range, with a good number in the easier grades, so there is something for beginners and for people projecting harder lines. The trees are open enough that the boulders catch light and tend to stay dry. The walk in is short, and the boulders sit close to the path.
nh_wiswall_boulders_aka_thompson_farm.parking_note: Space near the trailhead on Packers Falls Road is very tight; the roadside on Wiswall Road is the usual choice. Longer trail approaches from the farm side offer more room for cars.

nh_band_m_rock.blurb: A granite cliff in the Albany area of the White Mountains with mostly trad routes and a handful of bolted lines. Most climbs fall between 5.9 and 5.12, with a few easier ones. The cliff is complicated, so finding the right line can take some patience. It faces the sun and warms up early, which suits shoulder-season days, but bugs can be bad in warm weather and the climbing tends to improve as you go higher. The walk to the base is short.

nh_revolutionary_war_boulder.blurb: A roadside boulder in the woods outside Richmond, in the Monadnock region of southwestern New Hampshire. The granite is excellent, and the stone holds a deep set of problems, from easy warm-ups through a wide spread of mid-grades and up to some very hard lines in the V10 range and beyond. Walk in from the road on an old jeep track. The rock is best avoided when it is wet, and climbers are asked to go light on chalk and leave no tick marks.
nh_revolutionary_war_boulder.parking_note: A pullout on Route 32 a short way north of Fish Hatchery Road serves as the parking spot; an old jeep track leads into the woods to the main boulder.

nh_6_echo_roof.blurb: A section of Whitehorse Ledge in North Conway, named for the big roof that hangs over the middle of the wall. The climbs are short, one or two pitches of granite, mostly trad with a few bolted and top-rope options, with plenty between 5.9 and 5.11. Styles mix friction, steep face and cracks. Much of the wall sits under the roof and stays shaded and cooler, and it is usually quieter than the slabs nearby. From the slabs, a short trail along the base leads to the start.

nh_main_cliff_right.blurb: The outlying walls at the right-hand side of the Main Cliff at Rumney, a large and complicated area of fine-grained, very hard schist. The climbing is mostly short sport routes, with a handful of trad lines and a couple of winter ice routes. Grades spread across the range, with plenty in the 5.7 to 5.11 band and a few harder lines. Climbs here lean toward corners, aretes and technical moves rather than steep pump. Be aware of loose ground at the base of the neighboring main wall.

nj_main_wall_and_right_wall.blurb: The principal cliff at Allamuchy Mountain State Park in the northwest corner of the state. It is a drive-up, short-walk crag with mostly trad and top-rope climbing, mostly in the 5.5 to 5.10 range, plus a few harder routes. The wall is shady and tucked in the woods, which makes it a comfortable choice on hot summer days. Standard trad gear up to a number 3 cam works well, and tri-cams help in the flared cracks. Guide groups often use it on summer weekends.
nj_main_wall_and_right_wall.parking_note: Two small lots sit along County Route 604, a bit under two miles from Route 206; a footpath leads from there into the woods and reaches the cliff in a few minutes.
